record.original_question: Describe the extreme points of the class Σ0 consisting of all functions g in Σ with constant term b0 = 0. Springer (see Pommerenke [656, p. 183]) showed that every g in Σ0 whose omitted set has measure zero is an extreme point. Is this condition also necessary? (P. L. Duren)

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $\Sigma$ denote the class of functions
$$g(z) = z + b_0 + \frac{b_1}{z} + \frac{b_2}{z^2} + \cdots$$
that are univalent and meromorphic on the domain $\{z \in \mathbb{C} : |z| > 1\}$, and let $\Sigma_0 \subset \Sigma$ be the subclass of those $g$ with $b_0 = 0$. The class $\Sigma_0$ is a compact convex subset of the topological vector space of functions analytic on $\{|z|>1\}$ (with the topology of uniform convergence on compact subsets, after subtracting the $z$ term). For $g \in \Sigma_0$, let $E(g) = \mathbb{C} \setminus g(\{|z|>1\})$ denote the omitted set.

It is known that if the planar Lebesgue measure of $E(g)$ is zero, then $g$ is an extreme point of $\Sigma_0$ (i.e., $g$ cannot be written as $\tfrac{1}{2}(g_1 + g_2)$ with $g_1, g_2 \in \Sigma_0$ and $g_1 \neq g_2$).

Question: Is the converse true? That is, must every extreme point $g$ of $\Sigma_0$ satisfy $\operatorname{meas}_2(E(g)) = 0$? More generally, give a complete description of the extreme points of $\Sigma_0$.
artifact.status_search_result: Web searches did not turn up a definitive resolution of Duren's question on whether every extreme point of $\Sigma_0$ must have an omitted set of planar measure zero, nor a complete characterization of the extreme points of $\Sigma_0$. The problem appears to remain open, but no recent authoritative source clearly confirming its current status was found.

status_evidence.title: Generalized support points of the set of univalent functions
status_evidence.snippet: Every support point is a monotone slit mapping whose omitted arc is analytic; an example shows an extreme point which is not a support point.
status_evidence.claim: Research on extreme/support points in univalent function classes is ongoing, but no source found resolving the converse for $\Sigma_0$.
